data.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
data.summary:
Input: An array of k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order.
Output: A single merged linked list containing all elements from all lists in sorted order.
Rules: The output list must be formed by splicing together the nodes of the given lists.
constraints: The sum of lists[i].length will not exceed 10^4
Each list[i] is sorted in ascending order

data.reference_solution:
def mergeKLists(lists):
    all_vals = []
    for l in lists:
        curr = l
        while curr:
            all_vals.append(curr.val)
            curr = curr.next
    all_vals.sort()
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    curr = dummy
    for v in all_vals:
        curr.next = ListNode(v)
        curr = curr.next
    return dummy.next
data.reference_time_complexity: O(N log N) where N is the total number of nodes across all lists.
data.generator_code:
def generate(rng, n):
    k = max(0, min(n, 100))
    lists = []
    for _ in range(k):
        length = rng.randint(0, 10)
        vals = sorted([rng.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(length)])
        head = None
        curr = None
        for v in vals:
            node = ListNode(v)
            if not head:
                head = node
                curr = head
            else:
                curr.next = node
                curr = node
        lists.append(head)
    return [lists]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    k = min(n, 100)
    lists = []
    for i in range(k):
        vals = sorted([rng.randint(-1000, 1000) for _ in range(10)])
        head = None
        curr = None
        for v in vals:
            node = ListNode(v)
            if not head:
                head = node
                curr = head
            else:
                curr.next = node
                curr = node
        lists.append(head)
    return [lists]

data.key_insight: We can maintain a min-heap of size at most k containing the current head nodes of all non-empty lists. At each step, we pop the smallest element from the heap, append it to our result list, and push its next node (if any) into the heap.

steps.title: Initialize Min-Heap
steps.detail: Create a min-heap to store tuples of (node.val, index, node). The index is used as a tie-breaker to avoid comparing ListNode objects directly when values are equal.

steps.title: Seed the Heap
steps.detail: Iterate through the given list of linked lists. If a list is not empty, push its head node into the heap.

steps.title: Merge Lists
steps.detail: Create a dummy head for the result list. While the heap is not empty, pop the smallest node, append it to the current tail, and if the popped node has a next node, push that next node into the heap.

steps.title: Return Result
steps.detail: Return dummy.next as the head of the fully merged sorted linked list.

data.pattern_summary: Min-Heap (or Priority Queue) allows you to repeatedly find and extract the minimum element among a dynamic collection in logarithmic time, making it ideal for problems involving merging multiple sorted sequences.

pattern_options.name: Min-Heap
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Since we have multiple sorted lists, tracking their current minimums efficiently using a heap lets us build the final sorted list faster than sorting from scratch.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers works well when merging two lists, but scaling it directly to k lists becomes inefficient or cumbersome without a priority structure.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: A hash map helps with O(1) membership checks or frequencies, but it does not maintain sorted order or help merge ordered sequences.

pattern_options.name: Depth-first search
pattern_options.feedback: DFS explores graph or tree branches by going deep, which does not align with merging sequential sorted data.

signals.phrase: An array of k linked lists
signals.hint: Having multiple separate collections points to needing a way to coordinate between them simultaneously.
The internal order of each input can be leveraged instead of treating them as completely unstructured data.
The final output requires elements to be sequenced from smallest to largest.

data.brute_force_idea: Traverse every linked list to collect all node values into a single array, sort the entire array, and then build and return a brand new linked list from the sorted values.
data.brute_force_why: N is the total number of nodes across all lists. Collecting them takes O(N) time, sorting the complete array takes O(N log N) time, and rebuilding the linked list takes O(N) time.
data.bottleneck: Sorting all values together discards the fact that the individual input lists are already sorted.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how the input data is initially structured.
Ask yourself if you are throwing away useful ordering information by dumping everything into one flat list.
Think about how much work is repeated when you sort all elements from scratch instead of looking at just the current smallest candidates from each list.
data.brute_force_code:
def mergeKLists(lists):
    all_vals = []
    for l in lists:
        curr = l
        while curr:
            all_vals.append(curr.val)
            curr = curr.next
    all_vals.sort()
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    curr = dummy
    for v in all_vals:
        curr.next = ListNode(v)
        curr = curr.next
    return dummy.next

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach collects all nodes and sorts them from scratch, ignoring the fact that the input lists are already individually sorted. The optimized approach uses a min-heap to keep track of the smallest current element from each of the k lists at any given time. By always pulling the global minimum and adding the next element from that same list, we avoid a full re-sort and only do logarithmic work per node.

derivation.note: Iterates through the list of k heads to populate the initial heap array.
Turns the array of size at most k into a valid min-heap using heapify.
Extracts the minimum element from the heap, which takes logarithmic time relative to heap size k.
Pushes the next node from the exhausted list into the heap, maintaining heap size <= k.

data.time_summary: Lines 15 through 19 run once for every single node across all lists. Let N be the total number of nodes. Each node is popped and pushed once, and each heap operation takes O(log k) time. Thus, the total time complexity is O(N log k).
data.space_summary: The min-heap stores at most one node from each of the k lists at any given time. Therefore, the extra memory used is O(k).
data.takeaway: When merging multiple sorted sequences, use a min-heap to track the active head of each sequence. This reduces sorting overhead by processing elements in sorted order dynamically.
mistakes: Forgetting to check if a linked list is initially empty before pushing its head to the heap.
Not including a tie-breaker index (like 'i') in the heap tuples, which causes Python to throw an error if two linked list nodes have the same value.
Failing to advance and push the next node from the same list into the heap after popping an element.

data.overview: This algorithm merges k sorted linked lists efficiently using a min-heap. By always extracting the smallest node among the current heads of the lists, we build the final sorted list in O(N log k) time.
data.intuition: Imagine k lanes of traffic converging into a single road. At each junction, you look at the front car of each lane, pick the one with the lowest number, let it pass, and then the next car in that specific lane steps up to the front.

pitfalls: Forgetting to check if a list is initially empty before adding its head to the heap.
Failing to store the list index along with the node value in the tuple, which can cause comparison errors in Python if node values are identical.
Not advancing the current pointer correctly when appending nodes.
